role: Casting process engineer at a foundry
headline: A casting process engineer five years out of a degree in materials forming, running process at a pump-and-valve foundry in a Hebei casting cluster, where the pouring floor hits fifty degrees in summer and the furnaces go cold whenever autumn and winter smog alerts come
unit: A pump-and-valve casting foundry in the foundry park of a county-level city under Cangzhou, Hebei
city: A county-level city under Cangzhou, Hebei
education: Bachelor's degree (Materials Forming and Control Engineering)
level: You can design the process and the gating and risers for routine resin-sand and lost-foam castings on your own, and you can usually trace shrinkage and gas porosity to their cause. Your simulation software is an old version someone found online, and you're still learning the investment casting line the plant has just put in
intro: You studied materials forming in the provincial capital and came back to this foundry park near your home in Cangzhou. In five years you've gone from an assistant running drawings to designing the process on your own, and of the two hundred-odd workers in the plant, you're the only one who understands simulation. This year the environmental rules are tightening again, and the boss says it's upgrade or close. As of today, every heat of iron in this plant carries your signature.
salary_note: Estimate: a process engineer at a private foundry in a Hebei county-level city earns ¥7,000–8,000 a month, about seventy percent of the national figure. In months of production cuts during autumn and winter smog, there is only base pay; in good years there's a profit share at year end.

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Knocking out the shell and first visual inspection of the first casting

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Shift handover and checking conditions before the furnace is lit

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 11 related job listings nationwide (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: You leave home in the county town and drive twenty minutes to the foundry park. On both sides of the road are rows of sheds, and the air carries a faint smell of burnt sand. You've breathed it for five years and can't smell it anymore.

Morning meeting. The shop foreman says six valve bodies from yesterday's batch have shrinkage under the risers, and the customer is chasing the order. You carry a reject out into the sun, cut it open with an angle grinder, and the section is pocked with tiny holes.
Back at the office you start a simulation. On the old computer one solidification run takes four hours, so while it runs you move the risers around on the drawing.

To the melt shop for the furnace tap. The iron in the induction furnace is at 1,500 degrees. The old furnaceman takes a sample with a ladle; you take the spectrometer slip: carbon equivalent low, add a little recarburizer.

Lunch in the canteen. At the next table the boss is on the phone saying the environmental inspectors are coming next week to check fugitive emissions, and every shop is to keep its dust collectors running.

Pouring. In summer the pouring floor is over fifty degrees. You stand by the ladle in flame-retardant overalls, watching the iron go into the flasks ladle by ladle, flames leaping from the tops of the risers.
Shakeout and fettling. In a dust mask you watch the first casting at the shakeout table, knock off the gate, and shine a flashlight into the seams.

After dinner at home you watch a video a colleague elsewhere has sent: a die-casting machine of several thousand tonnes closes, and out comes a whole car underbody in one piece. You watch it three times.

ladder.title: Assistant Casting Engineer
ladder.focus: Work on the melt, molding and pouring floors and learn the rhythm of production; draw 2D and 3D rough-casting drawings, write the day-to-day work instructions, and help track down common surface defects. You move up on fast reactions on the floor and on standardizing drawings and procedures.

ladder.title: Casting Process Engineer
ladder.focus: Develop the process for routine products, such as chassis parts, gearbox housings and valve bodies, on your own; lead gating and riser design, optimize it with simulation, follow trial pours on the floor and bring first-article defects down. You move up on how efficiently you deliver good castings.

ladder.title: Senior Casting Process Engineer
ladder.focus: Take on the process for complex, difficult castings, such as thin-walled housings, large single-piece die castings and high-temperature pressure parts, and lead design-for-manufacture reviews; solve stubborn shrinkage and cracking, and drive cost-down and yield improvement. You move up on stable volume production of major new products.

ladder.title: Chief Casting Engineer
ladder.focus: Decide the casting routes for the whole plant or division, such as moving from sand to low-pressure casting or bringing in large single-piece die casting; set the company's process standards, lead digital upgrades of the lines and review major equipment investments. You build your name on overall yield and leadership in the industry.

ai_tasks.name: Shift handover and checking conditions before the furnace is lit
ai_tasks.how: AI can pull together the last heat's history, alarm logs and sensor readings and flag anomalies and risks. Whether the furnace is fit to light is judged on the spot by the engineer and the shop foreman, who sign and answer for it.

ai_tasks.name: Calculating the alloy charge and double-checking the weighing at the furnace
ai_tasks.how: AI can match barcodes to recipes, calculate the charge sheet, and catch wrong materials and out-of-tolerance weights. The real condition of master alloys and returns, and the check on the scales, still need someone watching, and coordinating with the storekeeper is still done by people.

ai_tasks.name: Pulling vacuum, heating and refining the melt
ai_tasks.how: AI can suggest heating curves from past heats, monitor vacuum and temperature and flag deviations. The engineer runs the vacuum induction furnace itself and handles anything abnormal; when something goes wrong, a person makes the call.

ai_tasks.name: Sampling the melt and fine-tuning composition
ai_tasks.how: AI can read the spectrometer results, quickly work out how much aluminum or other elements to add and suggest a second refining. The engineer decides, from the state of the furnace, whether to take its advice, and watches over the additions and refining.

ai_tasks.name: Trial pours of ceramic shells and optimizing process parameters
ai_tasks.how: AI can link mold-filling and solidification simulation, batch defect data and parameters, and suggest adjustments for the next heat. Pouring at high temperature and judgment on the spot are done by people, and the engineer sets the final parameters.

ai_tasks.name: Knocking out the shell and first visual inspection of the first casting
ai_tasks.how: Vibrating off the shell and safely cutting off the gates are hands-on work on the floor, and someone has to be there to answer for safety. AI image recognition can help spot surface defects, but judging the risk of shrinkage and distortion still rests on the engineer's experience.

ai_tasks.name: Reviewing the trial heat and archiving process data
ai_tasks.how: AI can combine sensor curves, lab reports and first-article inspection reports into a trial summary and traceability file. The engineer only spot-checks that the conclusions make sense and adds what experience says.

events.e_old_master: The old furnaceman told you to forget the spectrometer slip for a moment and look at the color of the iron and the sparks; when it turns whitish, it's hot enough. You checked him against an infrared thermometer for a month and found he was almost never wrong.
events.e_cae_win: A valve body with a complicated shape: you ran five versions of the gating system in simulation, and the very first heat came out good. The foreman tapped the casting and said this thing used to take three tries.
events.e_scrap: Half a batch of export pump housings leaked in pressure testing, and the customer sent back two truckloads. You went through the fractures one by one and finally traced it to too much moisture in the molding sand. Part of the fine came out of your pay.
events.e_lockdown: The first heavy-pollution alert of the winter, and the park shut its furnaces under emergency controls for twelve days. Orders piled up undelivered and the workers went home. Alone in the office, you revised the process cards for a new part four times.
events.e_inspection: Central environmental inspectors made an unannounced visit to the park, and two plants next door were sealed on the spot. Your dust collectors were running and your logs were in order. The boss took you out for drinks and said it was thanks to you making them fill in the records last month.
events.e_heat: July, and the pouring floor was over fifty degrees. You spent three days straight on the floor watching trial pours, and on the third afternoon everything went black and you crouched down where you stood. Workers carried you under a fan and poured a bottle of herbal heatstroke tonic into you.
events.e_love: A relative introduced you to a primary-school teacher in the county town. On your first meeting she asked why you smelled of burning. You said that's what casting smells like. She laughed and said she'd have to get used to it.
events.e_cupola: The old cupola furnace was finally torn down and replaced by two induction furnaces. On demolition day the old hands stood by smoking and said that furnace had been with the plant twenty years. You signed the operating procedure for the new ones.
events.e_wedding: You married in the county town. More than half the plant's workers came and filled eight tables. The boss gave a fat red envelope and said the groom was the plant's treasure.
events.e_export: A European pump-and-valve customer came to audit the plant, spent a whole day with an interpreter, and signed for a year of orders. At dinner the boss said if this order went well, everyone would get a share at year end.
events.e_baby: The day your child was born the plant was lighting the furnace, and outside the delivery room you took three calls from the shop floor. When the nurse brought the baby out, your phone was still ringing.
events.e_house: For your child's schooling later on, you bought a flat in Cangzhou city. From then on the commute added an hour a day, and on the drive you listened to the news, and pricked up your ears at the word “environment.”
events.e_classmate: A university classmate works at a company in the Yangtze River Delta that makes large single-piece die castings, and earns more than twice what you do. He posted a photo of the die-casting machine in the group chat and asked if you wanted to come. You didn't reply.
events.e_dust: At the plant's occupational health checkup, one of your lung-function numbers came back low. You switched to a better dust mask and never again complained it was stuffy on the floor.
events.e_pricewar: Several plants in the park started a price war, and the processing fee for a tonne of castings fell to cost. The boss told you to save iron on the risers. You ran the numbers for three days and told him any less and you'd get shrinkage.
events.e_ai_batch: The plant brought in an AI charge-calculation system that scans the returns and works out the charge sheet and additions automatically. Your job became checking its sums. Once it took a batch of rusty returns for good stock.
events.e_ai_vision: The fettling shop installed machine vision: castings pass under a camera, and surface defects are marked automatically. What's left for people is what the camera can't see: whether there's shrinkage inside, whether it rings right when you tap it.
events.e_son_boss: The boss's son came back from studying abroad to take over and wants a digital shop floor. The first thing he did was have all your process cards entered into the system. You had a row with him, then pulled two all-nighters with him.
events.e_ai_archive: Trial summaries and traceability files are now generated by the system: sensor curves, lab reports, first-article reports, packaged in one click. You just check the conclusion and add a line: on this heat, the furnaceman said the iron was sluggish.
events.e_apprentice: The assistant you trained designed the process for a part on his own for the first time, and on the day the mold was opened he was too nervous to look. You knocked off the gate for him. The section was sound. He smiled and said nothing.
events.e_father: Your father was a molder at another plant in the park all his life, and since retiring his cough hasn't cleared. You took him for tests at the hospital in the city and queued all morning.
events.e_back: Years of crouching on the shop floor over castings and hauling test bars, and your back has started to disobey. Getting down is easy; getting up, you hold on to a flask.

c_cae.title: Talk the boss into buying licensed simulation software
c_cae.situation: The plant's simulation software is an old version someone found online, and it often crashes on big castings. A licensed copy costs several hundred thousand yuan. The boss asks how much it will save in scrap a year, and you need numbers to answer.

options.label: Build the case, push the boss
options.result: You spent a month adding up two years of scrap and wrote a twelve-page proposal. The boss was silent for a long time, then signed, and said: if we buy it, you'd better earn it back.

options.label: Don't bother, go on experience
options.result: You didn't raise it. The old software stays, you rerun it when it crashes, big castings still mean trial and error, and the scrap rate is neither high nor low.

c_cert.title: Sit the foundry engineer evaluation
c_cert.situation: The foundry society's engineer evaluation is being held in the provincial capital this year: a theory exam and a process report, and it counts toward the intermediate professional title too. To become a Senior Casting Process Engineer you'll need it sooner or later, and preparing will take three months of weekends.

options.label: Sit it, weekends in the capital
options.result: You spent three months of weekends in a training room in the capital. The day it ended you ate a bowl of beef noodles at the station and thought it was the best you'd ever had.

options.label: Not yet
options.result: You kept your weekends for your family. The certificate slipped two years, and when titles were awarded you were further down the list.

c_newplant.title: Lead the process planning for the new plant
c_newplant.situation: As the environmental rules keep tightening, the boss has decided to borrow and move into the new green foundry park the city has built, and wants you to lead the process planning for the new plant: choose the furnaces, lay out the lines, set the dust controls. Get it right and you're head of technology; get it wrong and tens of millions in loans are sitting there.

options.label: Lead it
options.result: You spent a year going between equipment makers and design institutes. The day the new plant started up, the dust-collector outlet tested at half the legal limit.

options.label: Don't take it, stay in the old plant
options.result: The boss brought in an outside design institute. When the new plant opened, half the old hands didn't follow, and in the old plant you saw off the last heat of iron.

c_yangtze.title: Go to the Yangtze River Delta for large single-piece die casting
c_yangtze.situation: Your classmate's die-casting company is hiring, at double your pay, making rear underbodies for electric cars. It's high-pressure aluminum die casting, and much of the grey and ductile iron you know you'd have to learn again; you'd either move the family or come home once a month.

options.label: Go to the Delta
options.result: The first time you stood beside that machine of several thousand tonnes, the shock of the dies closing came up through the soles of your feet. The pay really did double, and you came home once a month.

options.label: Stay in Hebei
options.result: You stayed. Your classmate later became a supervisor, and once, on a trip to Hebei, he had dinner at your place and said your castings here are honest work.

c_ai.title: Be the master of the AI process platform, or not
c_ai.situation: The boss's son wants an AI process platform that links heat data, simulation results and defect records and suggests parameters for the next heat. He wants you to be the system's “master”: label the data, review its suggestions, and write the old hands' experience into rules.

options.label: Be its master
options.result: You spent most of a year turning five years of heat records into tables and writing down the cause of every reject. When the system started making suggestions, you were the only one in the plant who knew why it said what it said.

options.label: No, keep the experience in your own head
options.result: You said a machine can't learn the color of molten iron. The system went in anyway. You glance at its suggested parameters now and then, but mostly you still go and look at the furnace.

c_sqe.title: Join a carmaker as a supplier quality engineer
c_sqe.situation: A carmaker's purchasing quality department is hiring someone to audit its upstream foundries. They like that you understand process and can read defects; the pay is thirty percent higher, the job is in Tianjin, and you'd never set foot on a fifty-degree floor again. Only from now on, you'd be the one across the table finding fault with foundries.

options.label: Join the carmaker
options.result: You went to Tianjin with an audit checklist.
options.end: In a carmaker's work jacket you walk into one foundry after another, cut open a casting, look at the section, and know at a glance whether this heat was rushed.

options.label: Stay at the foundry
options.result: You said you still liked watching the iron. The job went to someone else, who later came to audit your plant once, and you walked him round for a whole day.

c_workshop.title: Become foundry shop manager, or stay technical
c_workshop.situation: The shop manager is retiring, and the boss wants you to take over: production planning, safety and wages for two hundred workers. The other path is to keep taking on the hard castings and stay on the technical track.

options.label: Take the shop
options.result: You started drawing up rotas, working out wages, dealing with injuries and arguments, and in summer keeping watch for heatstroke. The last time you designed gating yourself was three months ago.

options.label: Stay technical
options.result: You turned it down. The new manager came from another plant, and whenever there's a hard casting, he comes to you first.

c_chief.title: Run for Chief Casting Engineer
c_chief.situation: The plant has grown into a group and wants a Chief Casting Engineer to own the process routes of all three shops, and to decide whether to put in a low-pressure casting line: tens of millions in investment on your word. Your rival is a PhD brought in from outside.

options.label: Go for chief engineer
options.result: You wrote a sixty-page plan that was all about the scrap and the iron of the past fifteen years. When someone asked what made you the right person, you set a sectioned casting on the meeting table.

options.label: Leave it to the PhD
options.result: The PhD became chief engineer, and his first question was: where does this plant's scrap actually come from? You spent an afternoon telling him.

c_cae_consult.title: Move into simulation consulting
c_cae_consult.situation: A company that makes casting simulation software wants you as an applications engineer, consulting and training foundries all over the country, based in Beijing, never on the shop floor. You know what a foundry really lacks; the people who write the code don't.

options.label: Go into simulation consulting
options.result: You left the shop floor and carried a laptop to foundries across half of China.
options.end: In somebody else's meeting room you slow down the solidification simulation on the screen, point to a red spot and say: here. It'll shrink here.

options.label: Stay on the floor
options.result: You said no. That afternoon you were back on the pouring floor, watching a ladle of iron go slowly into the flask.

endings.retire: On the last day you hand over thirty-odd years of process cards and simulation files to the young engineer taking your place, more than twenty thousand files on the hard drive. You go and stand on the pouring floor one last time; the red glow of the iron on your face is as hot as ever. When you walk out the gate, the sky over the park is blue.
endings.burnout: That summer everything went black on the pouring floor again, and this time an ambulance took you. After you came out of hospital the boss moved you to the office to look after the technical files, off the floor for good. You leave on time every day, and passing the shop door you still stop to breathe in that smell of burnt sand.

past: Your father was a molder at a plant in the park, and every day he came home with sand in his hair. In your last year of middle school you took him his lunch at the plant and saw molten iron poured into a flask for the first time, its red light filling the whole shed.

The gaokao (college entrance exam) got you into an engineering university in the provincial capital. When you filled in your choices your father said: study something to do with casting, we've no shortage of plants round here. You put down Materials Forming and Control Engineering.

In third-year metalworking practice you made a small sand mold yourself, and the aluminum part that came out was full of gas holes. The teacher said casting is a craft of fighting gas. You remembered it.

For your graduation project you did a shrinkage analysis in simulation software and for the first time watched on screen how metal solidifies, bit by bit. You thought it was one of the most beautiful things you'd ever seen.

At graduation your classmates went to carmakers and die-casters in the Yangtze River Delta. You came home and joined this plant in the park as an assistant engineer, on ¥4,500 a month, living with your parents.

You designed the process for a part on your own for the first time, a grey-iron pump cover. The first heat had three castings with cold shuts. You spent two days crouched on the floor and moved the ingate.

late.pension_note: Estimate: private foundries pay into the basic pension for company employees on a low contribution base, so the pension comes to about forty percent of your final monthly pay. There is no company annuity.
scenes: For the first few days of retirement you still woke before six and checked the forecast for smog alerts first thing. Only later did you remember that whether the furnaces run is no longer your business.
A small plant in the park asked you to consult two days a week, looking at rejects and adjusting gates. The owner said one look from you was worth three of their trials.

Your child finished university in another city, studying artificial intelligence, and wants to build algorithms for industrial inspection. He asked what shrinkage in a casting looks like, and you drew him a picture.
On the estate you ran into the old furnaceman, past eighty now and hard of hearing. You sat on a bench for half a day and talked only about which heat of iron in which year.

Looking after the technical files in the office, you mark up the young engineers' process cards every day, dense with red ink. Behind your back they call you the old fossil, and the cards you've corrected are all right.
Your health slowly came back. At weekends you took your child to fly a kite in the park. The sky was very blue, and you said when you were small the sky here was nothing like this clean.
When the time came you retired. The pension isn't much. You grow a row of chili plants on the balcony and go to look at them every morning.
In the first year off the shop floor, without the smell of burnt sand, you felt oddly out of place, and sometimes drove out to the edge of the park just to circle it.
You found your feet in the new place. When you go back to the old plant, the workers still call you the young engineer, though you haven't been young for a long time.
The assistant you once trained became the plant's chief engineer. He called to say they'd put in a low-pressure casting line, and asked if you'd come and watch the first heat.

Later half the plants in the park were gone, and those that stayed had electric furnaces, dust controls and AI systems. But when the iron goes into the flask, someone still has to stand beside it and watch.
There are a few small white marks on the back of your hand from iron that splashed when you were young. A grandchild asked what they were, and you said they were stars that flew out of the furnace.

closing.retire: Many years later, on a winter day, you walk down a street in the county town under a deep blue sky without a trace of haze. You think of those winters with the furnaces cold, of the color of the iron, and you stand at the corner for a long time looking at the sheds in the distance.
closing.burnout: Many years later you watch a grandchild playing in a sandpit in the park. He turns out a castle from a little bucket and asks if it looks right. You crouch down and dig a small hollow in the top of the castle for him, and tell him that's called a riser.
closing.end: Many years later you find your university textbook on casting process in the bookcase, and between its pages a yellowed screenshot of a solidification simulation. You look at it for a while, then tuck it back on the same page.

stages: The process for routine parts is yours from start to finish. When a customer sends a 3D model, you build the rough casting and add machining stock in UG, design the gating and risers, run the solidification simulation, then write the process card and work instructions. On trial day you stand by the molding line and the pouring floor, and when the first casting comes out, you're the first to cut it open. The foreman and the furnacemen listen to you, and pick holes in you too.

The hard castings start coming your way: thin-walled housings, high-pressure valve bodies, large castings. You chair design-for-manufacture reviews for new products and argue a draft angle with the customer's engineers on video calls; when scrap rises you take your assistants through a PFMEA and write the 8D report. Two assistants work to the processes you sign.

Your job is the whole plant's process routes: which parts stay in resin sand, which move to low pressure, whose equipment to buy for the new line. Half your time is in meeting rooms with investment models and equipment makers' proposals; the other half you still spend on the floor, reading the overall yield report and seeing which shop is dragging again.
work: A customer sent the 3D model of a pump housing. In UG you added machining stock and draft and exported the rough-casting drawing to the pattern shop. The patternmaker phoned to say the core print was too thin.
The furnaceman brought you a spectrometer slip: silicon high. On the charge sheet you cut the returns by fifty kilos, signed it, and told him to charge it that way.
Watching the molding line, you saw a worker set a chill a finger's width off. You stopped the line and chalked a circle on the sand mold.
On a video call the customer's engineer insisted on zero draft. You held simulation screenshots and three scrapped samples up to the camera, and in the end he agreed to one degree.
With two assistants you worked through an 8D report on shrinkage in a valve body, drawing a fishbone on the whiteboard. At the sixth bone, an assistant said: pouring temperature.
A European customer came for a process audit. The auditor went through the IATF 16949 checklist item by item, and you walked him from the melt shop to fettling, answering questions for four hours.

An equipment maker's salesman brought a proposal for a low-pressure casting line. On the investment model you changed the payback period from three years to five, and said: I don't believe your yield figure.
At the monthly quality meeting you put every shop's yield report on the wall and named Shop Two. Afterward you took its manager to dinner on your own.
The new PhD engineer showed you his multiphysics simulation. When you'd finished looking, you asked him: have you ever stood at the furnace for a whole day?
